lines.watchItem: The largest cloud customers keep raising 2026 spending plans and NVIDIA's data-center sales hit a record, so leading-edge wafer-start planning faces order flow running well ahead of what the chain can deliver. Watch whether cloud backlog keeps growing faster than deliveries.

Advanced packaging is fully booked through 2026 with 52-to-78-week lead times and allocation running into mid-2027, so packaging slots, not wafers, set how much accelerator revenue can actually ship. The gap is expected to narrow from about 20% to about 10% by end-2026 as capacity climbs toward 125,000-130,000 wafers a month.

Three customers take more than 85% of advanced-packaging output, with one of them at roughly 60%, and that same customer is reported to be weighing a shift of some next-generation output to Intel's packaging. Any single order cut or route change lands on capacity that is hard to refill.

Custom AI chips are growing about 44.6% this year against 16.1% for merchant GPUs and are projected near 28% of the market, while AMD lands gigawatt-scale rack commitments. The leading-node customer base is shifting from one dominant merchant vendor toward a mix of AMD plus custom silicon that runs almost entirely through two design houses.

AI demand is spreading beyond GPUs into custom chips, networking and power parts, filling capacity across 8-inch, 12-inch and packaging lines, and TSMC reported a 67.7% gross margin with full-year growth guidance raised above 40%. That combination points to firm pricing power for the foundry as long as the demand-supply gap stays wide.

Intel Foundry revenue rose 31% to $5.8 billion, it named Fortinet as an external customer, lifted capital spending above $20 billion, and detailed an inference GPU that uses standard memory to sidestep advanced packaging entirely. That is a second-source route forming around the exact capacity that is scarcest today.

China policy moved from denial to case-by-case review for H200-class parts, yet NVIDIA's China revenue halved to $4.55 billion, licensed shipments remain trivial under a 25% tariff, and smuggling enforcement is widening. Policy sets a capped ceiling on addressable demand, while a further $100 billion US commitment shifts where new capacity sits.

A visible slice of today's order book rests on vendor credit and borrowing: NVIDIA is negotiating backstops measured in hundreds of billions, Alphabet funded the quarter with equity and notes while posting its first negative free cash flow, and CoreWeave carries debt at 5.4 times equity. That financing chain is where a demand reversal would show up first in wafer-start planning.
